decisions.reason: “Confined to” preserves the sense while reading naturally.
The rearrangement keeps the location, distance, and comparison intact.
“Crunch” is a plausible rendering of the source’s impact sound.
SOL drops the weapons’ reciprocal flight toward each other; BASE preserves that action.
“Each” makes the implied distribution across the rotting bodies explicit.
The recast preserves the fear and the sound restoring the soldiers’ focus.
Striking the drum with all their might preserves the source’s forceful action.
“Snapped” naturally conveys the flag’s vigorous flutter at the command.
Dropping “the” does not change the troop count or movement.
The hedgehog-spine comparison preserves the dense spear formation.
“Across the field” preserves the scattered eruptions in natural English.
“Didn’t suffer so much as a scratch” preserves the monsters’ resistance.
SOL changes bodies becoming mere flesh into men being thrown like meat, altering the source’s image.
“Relentless” preserves the charge’s persistence without changing its action.
SOL’s singular “it” misstates the plural monsters being cut down.
Omitting “the” before green blood changes no meaning.
“Severed” conveys the monsters’ fragmented corpses in this context.
The shortened parallel phrase keeps both the armor and the man in focus.
“With unmistakable loyalty and reverence” preserves the soldiers’ feeling.
The sentence break preserves the ruler’s titles and adds no new claim.
The recast keeps the emperor’s practical response to the urgent situation.
The rearranged sentence preserves the monster’s dive, folded wings, and shudder.
The challenge preserves the rebuke in natural spoken English.
“Look upon” preserves the soldiers’ awe and reluctance to gaze at him.
The adverb placement preserves their willingness to give their lives.
“Voices” makes the implied source of the growing roar explicit without changing its scale.
Naming the emperor as the one answering preserves the action.
The punctuation change leaves the request and its sequence intact.
The concise description preserves the officer’s respectful, unflinching manner.
“Its laws” clearly refers to the imperial house and preserves the contrast.
SOL drops the source’s explicit characterization of the answer as disrespectful.
The recast preserves his exceptional service protecting the imperial house.
“Corrected him” naturally refers to the emperor’s earlier words in context.
“I had to” preserves the sense in natural dialogue.
“Safely in the rear” preserves the officer’s point about the emperor’s proper position.
The recast preserves the foolish-question, wise-answer exchange.
Dropping the repeated “here” preserves the parallel actions.
“Out of humanity” loses the specific compassion for his people expressed by 인의.
“Compassion” preserves the source’s repeated theme of care for the people.
The natural phrasing preserves his military talent and Dark Heaven’s shadow over the imperial house.
“The only way” preserves the belief that coldness was the sole means to solve every problem.
Removing the comma after “until” preserves the timing and reads smoothly.
Removing “simply” does not change his determined advance.
The question preserves the proposed explanation of his actions.
“No” naturally rejects the bravery explanation in context.
SOL changes the comparison from feeling more fear and pain than others to more than anyone, and weakens compassion into “the human thing.”
The tense and verb changes preserve the path reaching and bringing people here.
The split sentence preserves the court’s likely reaction and the emperor’s action.
The full verb form is a stylistic change with no shift in meaning.
The source asks whether his resolve remains unchanged, not simply whether he changed his mind.
SOL drops the contrastive “in return,” which marks the officer’s obligation alongside the emperor’s withdrawal.
“Withdraw forward, not back” preserves the deliberate reversal.
The exclamation mark preserves the source’s startled reaction.
The source again asks whether his resolve remains unchanged; SOL instead asks if he changed his mind.
“Knelt” preserves the action in concise natural English.
The recast preserves the thousand guards’ unified roar and its effect on the battlefield.
SOL removes the source’s emphasis that the cry reached even the true enemy.
SOL adds a separate sound effect that duplicates the following paragraph’s sound.
The rearrangement preserves the armor’s appearance and the sound of its movement.
The recast preserves the red eyes and corpse stench while reading naturally.
“The equal of” preserves the comparison to a Supreme Peak master.
The split preserves the trembling eyes and the emperor’s ensuing cry.
“Crunch” is a plausible rendering of the source’s impact sound.
“Across the battlefield” preserves the lights appearing throughout it.
The reordered actions preserve the twelve masters’ arrival and their deep bow.
“Directly serving the imperial house” naturally conveys their direct imperial allegiance.
The source asks whether anyone could dare predict victory; SOL changes prediction to hope.
“He” clearly refers to the Son of Heaven established in the surrounding passage.
The wording change leaves the consequence of retreat unchanged.
“The world around him” narrows the source’s claim that one man changed more than this world.
“Accepting” preserves the source’s receipt of the Maoshan Sect’s martial arts.
“Like everyone else here” preserves the comparison.
SOL drops the source’s “once again,” losing the repeated awakening.
Naming Jin Taekyung clarifies the already established antecedent without adding information.
The split preserves the connection between the lack of decorum and the freedom it makes clear.
“Stretched out behind him” preserves the golden trail.
The recast preserves the streaks crossing the sky and its unnoticed darkening.
“So why?” preserves the wondering question in natural English.
The source says he pressed down on his chest; SOL adds a hand and changes the physical action.
SOL adds “afterward,” an explicit temporal link absent from the source.
The source says he could not sleep even after night gave way to dawn; SOL’s “not when” changes that temporal relation.
Removing the comma does not change the sequence of travel and arrival.
